romania.title: Un cercetător afirmă că a rezolvat ipoteza Riemann, cu AI. Soluția celei mai importante probleme de matematică are 250.000 de pagini
romania.summary: Cercetătorul Levent Alpöge a afirmat, vineri, că a rezolvat ipoteza Riemann, considerată de unii drept cea mai importantă problemă de matematică din lume, cu ajutorul unui model de inteligenţă artificială (AI) dezvoltat de Anthropic. Într-o răsturnare de situaţie, câteva ore mai târziu, un profesor de matematică de la Universitatea Stanford, Ravi Vakil, a relatat că un student din cadrul aceleiaşi facultăţi a prezentat, în mod independent, propria sa demonstraţie. Ambii au fost contactaţi de AFP, dar nu au oferit un răspuns imediat, scrie News.ro.

medical.title: Mental health diagnoses rise with medical complexity, chronicity in children
medical.summary: The prevalence of mental health (MH) diagnoses increases with increasing medical complexity and chronicity in Medicaid-enrolled children, according to a study published in Pediatrics.

medical.title: Flu vaccine effectiveness often weaker than advertised, study finds
medical.summary: New research suggests health officials may be overselling the protective power of the annual flu shot—but that doesn't mean folks should skip it, researchers added. The new analysis finds the influenza vaccine is often less protective than the 40% to 60% effectiveness against infection that's routinely stated, according to researchers from the University of Maryland.

medical.title: Your genes might boost risk for high cholesterol
medical.summary: Frustrated that your cholesterol levels aren't budging for the better? You may have your genes to blame, a new study finds.

medical.title: Hair pulling, skin picking and nail biting are common in young people and cause significant distress
medical.summary: The study found that body-focused repetitive behaviors (BFRBs), as they are known, can be a significant source of distress, particularly among young people who also experienced anxiety, depression and bullying.

medical.title: Less than half of TikTok videos on RSV prevention offer high-quality info, paper notes
medical.summary: Many people rely on social media to learn more about health conditions and trends. A study published in Vaccine that examined TikTok videos about respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) prevention—including the maternal vaccine (Abrysvo) and the long-acting antibody nirsevimab (Beyfortus) for infants—finds that only 47% present high-quality information.

medical.title: Researchers uncover the mechanisms of adhesion formation after thoracic surgery
medical.summary: Intrathoracic adhesions can develop after thoracic surgery and increase the risk of complications during repeat surgery. However, the detailed molecular mechanisms underlying their formation have remained unclear. In a Letter published in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy, a team from Japan aimed to establish an animal model that closely reproduces pleural adhesions seen in patients and to identify key cells and signaling pathways involved in adhesion formation. The goal was to find new methods to prevent adhesions after thoracic surgery.

medical.title: Patients give dental implants high marks after 40 years
medical.summary: Nearly 40 years after receiving dental implants and crowns, patients remain highly satisfied with how well they function. Their views on appearance are more mixed, according to a study from the University of Gothenburg, Sweden.

medical.title: Improved mapping reveals location of small molecules in the brain
medical.summary: Hsi-Chun Chao, a postdoctoral researcher at the Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, developed a new methodology to map the locations of and differentiate nearly identical molecules in the brain.

medical.title: Metastatic pancreatic cancer responds well to treatment with combination of daraxonrasib and chemotherapy
medical.summary: Daraxonrasib combined with chemotherapy caused substantial tumor shrinkage in patients with pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body, according to new results from a Phase I/II clinical trial.

medical.title: Heart rhythm data reveal early signs of heart disease before conventional measures
medical.summary: The heart does not beat like a regular clock. Even at rest, the time between successive heartbeats continuously varies. Researchers at Tampere and Stanford universities have shown that the patterns of these subtle variations can reveal the early effects of cardiomyopathy, which is a hereditary heart disease. The paper is published in the journal Circulation: Arrhythmia and Electrophysiology.

medical.title: Immune aging blueprint offers new clues to fighting cancer
medical.summary: A new study from Monash University has uncovered a genetic blueprint of immune aging, shedding light on why our bodies become less effective at fighting cancer and infections as we grow older. Published in Science Immunology, the preclinical study identified genetic changes that cause aging immune cells to become less effective, helping to explain why older people are more susceptible to cancer and experience more frequent and severe infections.

medical.title: Nearly half of adults over 70 benefited from exercise training across several areas of physical function
medical.summary: A yearlong exercise program improved physical function among adults aged over 70, but the benefits varied considerably between individuals. A study conducted at the University of Jyväskylä highlights that the success of exercise interventions should not be evaluated using a single outcome measure, as positive changes may occur in different aspects of physical function.

medical.title: Cell biologists uncover key mechanism behind a rare cause of childhood epilepsy
medical.summary: University of Liverpool scientists have discovered how a protein linked to a severe form of childhood epilepsy is positioned within nerve cells, providing new insights into a rare genetic neurological disorder.

medical.title: Inner ear study challenges canonical understanding of hearing
medical.summary: New research offers a new understanding of how the inner ear processes sound, which could lead to improvements in hearing technology like cochlear implants.

medical.title: Can psychedelics improve decision-making?
medical.summary: For the one-in-five Americans with a mental health condition, the options for treatment aren't too much different from what they were half a century ago. Most medicines for psychiatric disorders were first pioneered in the 1950s.

medical.title: Custom MRI tool could show within weeks if pancreatic cancer treatment is working
medical.summary: About 60% of people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer don't qualify for surgery because their disease is too advanced. For these patients, treatment typically begins with chemotherapy, in the hope that the tumor will shrink enough to be surgically removed, which offers the best chance of long-term survival. A new clinical trial at The Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center—Arthur G. James Cancer Hospital and Richard J. Solove Research Institute (OSUCCC—James) is testing a custom imaging tool designed to measure much earlier whether that chemotherapy is working, so treatment can change quickly if it is not.

medical.title: Transgender consumers can face harm simply by trying to access everyday services, research finds
medical.summary: Transgender consumers can experience discrimination and psychological harm when carrying out everyday tasks such as changing their name, visiting a gym or accessing banking and health care, according to new research from the University of Bath.

medical.title: Open-source platform combines brain commands, spinal circuits and muscle responses in one simulation
medical.summary: Immense progress has been made in recent years in developing assistive systems for people who are paralyzed. However, the underlying neuromotor processes—from the brain's commands through the neural circuits in the spinal cord to the activation of the muscles—have so far been mostly studied in isolation. Researchers at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) and their partners in Brazil have developed the MyoGen platform, which integrates these processes into a single simulation. The model, presented in the journal Nature Communications, is freely accessible and is intended to support both clinical research and the optimization of medical devices.

science.title: Babies in ancient Greek colony started solid food at 3 months but nursed for nearly 4 years, chemical signatures suggest
science.summary: Over 2,500 years ago, Himera was a Greek colony inhabited by local Sicilians, Phoenicians and Greeks. Despite their diverse cultural backgrounds, they all shared one thing: they began weaning their babies early and continued for a long time.

science.title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
science.summary: Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.

science.title: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
science.summary: Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.

science.title: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved
science.summary: A mysterious skeleton discovered in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally be identified after more than 150 years. New dating evidence suggests the remains belonged to a high-ranking medieval abbot who was buried inside a centuries-old recycled Roman coffin.

science.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
science.summary: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.

science.title: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is
science.summary: Scientists cannot agree on what science actually is, and a new study finds their views are surprisingly more divided than those of the general public. The findings could help explain public frustration with scientific uncertainty and raise questions about how artificial intelligence might reshape future discoveries.

science.title: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
science.summary: The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.

science.title: Fermi's 14-year all-sky map bridges astronomy's elusive 'MeV gap'
science.summary: Gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot. We've always had trouble measuring them in the "megaelectronvolt" (MeV) energy range, which astronomers have taken to calling the "MeV gap." But a new paper from an international group of scientists working with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) Collaboration, recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series, takes a stab at closing that gap by identifying 450 cosmic sources in the 20–200 MeV range, providing the clearest view of low-energy gamma rays ever.

science.title: From screens in class to smart glasses, Norway rethinks new technologies
science.summary: Three years ago, a schoolteacher in Norway was reprimanded for putting his pupils' iPads aside to return to pen and paper. Now, the whole country is rethinking its approach to new technologies.

environment.summary: Japan has “tremendous potential” for offshore wind power, according to the national government and experts. But achieving that potential means overcoming major hurdles. environment.title: A mysterious 4,000-year-old wall is rewriting North Africa’s history
environment.summary: A remarkable 4,000-year-old defensive structure discovered in Morocco is rewriting what scientists thought they knew about ancient North African civilizations. The massive fortifications reveal unexpectedly sophisticated prehistoric societies and suggest that the region played a much greater role in Mediterranean history than previously recognized.

mix_items.title: Un cercetător afirmă că a rezolvat ipoteza Riemann, cu AI. Soluția celei mai importante probleme de matematică are 250.000 de pagini
mix_items.summary: Cercetătorul Levent Alpöge a afirmat, vineri, că a rezolvat ipoteza Riemann, considerată de unii drept cea mai importantă problemă de matematică din lume, cu ajutorul unui model de inteligenţă artificială (AI) dezvoltat de Anthropic. Într-o răsturnare de situaţie, câteva ore mai târziu, un profesor de matematică de la Universitatea Stanford, Ravi Vakil, a relatat că un student din cadrul aceleiaşi facultăţi a prezentat, în mod independent, propria sa demonstraţie. Ambii au fost contactaţi de AFP, dar nu au oferit un răspuns imediat, scrie News.ro.

mix_items.title: Babies in ancient Greek colony started solid food at 3 months but nursed for nearly 4 years, chemical signatures suggest
mix_items.summary: Over 2,500 years ago, Himera was a Greek colony inhabited by local Sicilians, Phoenicians and Greeks. Despite their diverse cultural backgrounds, they all shared one thing: they began weaning their babies early and continued for a long time.

mix_items.title: De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze
mix_items.summary: Descoperă povestea lui Darius și cum sprijinul educațional oferit de Fundația Inocenți l-a ajutat să capete încredere în sine și să își urmeze visurile. The post De la timiditate la încredere: povestea unui tânăr care îndrăznește să viseze appeared first on Fundația Inocenți .

mix_items.title: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it
mix_items.summary: Time may be far stranger than we realize, and scientists have proposed a way to detect clocks experiencing multiple flows of time simultaneously. Using atomic clocks with dramatically enhanced sensitivity, researchers hope to reveal a never-before-observed quantum effect that could transform our understanding of time and gravity.

mix_items.title: A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath
mix_items.summary: Astronomers have witnessed a spectacular cosmic collision in the Andromeda galaxy, where a small star spiraled into a giant star 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, triggering a violent eruption. NASA’s James Webb Space Telescope captured the aftermath just 47 days later, revealing new details about how two stars can merge into one.

mix_items.title: Who was buried in Westminster Abbey's Roman coffin? A 150-year mystery may be solved
mix_items.summary: A mysterious skeleton discovered in a Roman sarcophagus at Westminster Abbey may finally be identified after more than 150 years. New dating evidence suggests the remains belonged to a high-ranking medieval abbot who was buried inside a centuries-old recycled Roman coffin.

mix_items.title: A 50-year-old theory about evolution may have been wrong all along
mix_items.summary: A decades-old theory suggesting that evolution protects its most important genes from mutations has been dealt a major blow. An extensive new analysis of mutations in bacteria and yeast found no evidence that essential genes mutate less frequently than other genes. Researchers say earlier studies may have been misled by harmful mutations that disappeared through natural selection before scientists could detect them.

mix_items.title: Even scientists can't agree on what science actually is
mix_items.summary: Scientists cannot agree on what science actually is, and a new study finds their views are surprisingly more divided than those of the general public. The findings could help explain public frustration with scientific uncertainty and raise questions about how artificial intelligence might reshape future discoveries.

mix_items.title: Scientists say the human family tree may need a radical rewrite
mix_items.summary: The human family tree may need a major overhaul. New research from Monash University challenges the traditional classification of our ancient ancestors, arguing that species such as Australopithecus and Paranthropus should be grouped within our own genus, Homo. As scientists uncover more fossils and analyze evolutionary relationships, the boundaries that once separated these ancient relatives are becoming increasingly difficult to defend.

mix_items.title: Fermi's 14-year all-sky map bridges astronomy's elusive 'MeV gap'
mix_items.summary: Gamma rays, the most high-energy type of electromagnetic radiation in the universe, have always had a blind spot. We've always had trouble measuring them in the "megaelectronvolt" (MeV) energy range, which astronomers have taken to calling the "MeV gap." But a new paper from an international group of scientists working with the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT) Collaboration, recently published in The Astrophysical Journal Supplement Series, takes a stab at closing that gap by identifying 450 cosmic sources in the 20–200 MeV range, providing the clearest view of low-energy gamma rays ever.

mix_items.title: From screens in class to smart glasses, Norway rethinks new technologies
mix_items.summary: Three years ago, a schoolteacher in Norway was reprimanded for putting his pupils' iPads aside to return to pen and paper. Now, the whole country is rethinking its approach to new technologies.

mix_items.title: Mental health diagnoses rise with medical complexity, chronicity in children
mix_items.summary: The prevalence of mental health (MH) diagnoses increases with increasing medical complexity and chronicity in Medicaid-enrolled children, according to a study published in Pediatrics.

mix_items.title: Flu vaccine effectiveness often weaker than advertised, study finds
mix_items.summary: New research suggests health officials may be overselling the protective power of the annual flu shot—but that doesn't mean folks should skip it, researchers added. The new analysis finds the influenza vaccine is often less protective than the 40% to 60% effectiveness against infection that's routinely stated, according to researchers from the University of Maryland.

mix_items.title: Your genes might boost risk for high cholesterol
mix_items.summary: Frustrated that your cholesterol levels aren't budging for the better? You may have your genes to blame, a new study finds.

mix_items.title: Hair pulling, skin picking and nail biting are common in young people and cause significant distress
mix_items.summary: The study found that body-focused repetitive behaviors (BFRBs), as they are known, can be a significant source of distress, particularly among young people who also experienced anxiety, depression and bullying.

mix_items.title: Less than half of TikTok videos on RSV prevention offer high-quality info, paper notes
mix_items.summary: Many people rely on social media to learn more about health conditions and trends. A study published in Vaccine that examined TikTok videos about respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) prevention—including the maternal vaccine (Abrysvo) and the long-acting antibody nirsevimab (Beyfortus) for infants—finds that only 47% present high-quality information.

mix_items.title: Researchers uncover the mechanisms of adhesion formation after thoracic surgery
mix_items.summary: Intrathoracic adhesions can develop after thoracic surgery and increase the risk of complications during repeat surgery. However, the detailed molecular mechanisms underlying their formation have remained unclear. In a Letter published in Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy, a team from Japan aimed to establish an animal model that closely reproduces pleural adhesions seen in patients and to identify key cells and signaling pathways involved in adhesion formation. The goal was to find new methods to prevent adhesions after thoracic surgery.

mix_items.title: Patients give dental implants high marks after 40 years
mix_items.summary: Nearly 40 years after receiving dental implants and crowns, patients remain highly satisfied with how well they function. Their views on appearance are more mixed, according to a study from the University of Gothenburg, Sweden.

mix_items.title: Improved mapping reveals location of small molecules in the brain
mix_items.summary: Hsi-Chun Chao, a postdoctoral researcher at the Beckman Institute for Advanced Science and Technology at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, developed a new methodology to map the locations of and differentiate nearly identical molecules in the brain.

mix_items.title: Metastatic pancreatic cancer responds well to treatment with combination of daraxonrasib and chemotherapy
mix_items.summary: Daraxonrasib combined with chemotherapy caused substantial tumor shrinkage in patients with pancreatic cancer that had spread to other parts of the body, according to new results from a Phase I/II clinical trial.

mix_items.title: Heart rhythm data reveal early signs of heart disease before conventional measures
mix_items.summary: The heart does not beat like a regular clock. Even at rest, the time between successive heartbeats continuously varies. Researchers at Tampere and Stanford universities have shown that the patterns of these subtle variations can reveal the early effects of cardiomyopathy, which is a hereditary heart disease. The paper is published in the journal Circulation: Arrhythmia and Electrophysiology.

mix_items.title: Immune aging blueprint offers new clues to fighting cancer
mix_items.summary: A new study from Monash University has uncovered a genetic blueprint of immune aging, shedding light on why our bodies become less effective at fighting cancer and infections as we grow older. Published in Science Immunology, the preclinical study identified genetic changes that cause aging immune cells to become less effective, helping to explain why older people are more susceptible to cancer and experience more frequent and severe infections.

mix_items.title: Nearly half of adults over 70 benefited from exercise training across several areas of physical function
mix_items.summary: A yearlong exercise program improved physical function among adults aged over 70, but the benefits varied considerably between individuals. A study conducted at the University of Jyväskylä highlights that the success of exercise interventions should not be evaluated using a single outcome measure, as positive changes may occur in different aspects of physical function.

mix_items.title: Cell biologists uncover key mechanism behind a rare cause of childhood epilepsy
mix_items.summary: University of Liverpool scientists have discovered how a protein linked to a severe form of childhood epilepsy is positioned within nerve cells, providing new insights into a rare genetic neurological disorder.

mix_items.title: Inner ear study challenges canonical understanding of hearing
mix_items.summary: New research offers a new understanding of how the inner ear processes sound, which could lead to improvements in hearing technology like cochlear implants.

mix_items.title: Can psychedelics improve decision-making?
mix_items.summary: For the one-in-five Americans with a mental health condition, the options for treatment aren't too much different from what they were half a century ago. Most medicines for psychiatric disorders were first pioneered in the 1950s.

mix_items.title: Custom MRI tool could show within weeks if pancreatic cancer treatment is working
mix_items.summary: About 60% of people diagnosed with pancreatic cancer don't qualify for surgery because their disease is too advanced. For these patients, treatment typically begins with chemotherapy, in the hope that the tumor will shrink enough to be surgically removed, which offers the best chance of long-term survival. A new clinical trial at The Ohio State University Comprehensive Cancer Center—Arthur G. James Cancer Hospital and Richard J. Solove Research Institute (OSUCCC—James) is testing a custom imaging tool designed to measure much earlier whether that chemotherapy is working, so treatment can change quickly if it is not.

mix_items.title: Transgender consumers can face harm simply by trying to access everyday services, research finds
mix_items.summary: Transgender consumers can experience discrimination and psychological harm when carrying out everyday tasks such as changing their name, visiting a gym or accessing banking and health care, according to new research from the University of Bath.

mix_items.title: Open-source platform combines brain commands, spinal circuits and muscle responses in one simulation
mix_items.summary: Immense progress has been made in recent years in developing assistive systems for people who are paralyzed. However, the underlying neuromotor processes—from the brain's commands through the neural circuits in the spinal cord to the activation of the muscles—have so far been mostly studied in isolation. Researchers at Friedrich-Alexander-Universität Erlangen-Nürnberg (FAU) and their partners in Brazil have developed the MyoGen platform, which integrates these processes into a single simulation. The model, presented in the journal Nature Communications, is freely accessible and is intended to support both clinical research and the optimization of medical devices.

mix_items.title: Where family foundations can help marine conservation
mix_items.summary: COP17 ended in Armenia amid disappointment over the lack of concrete measures to reduce biodiversity loss by 2030. Finance was a sore point. Philanthropy is only a small part of that picture, but foundations can take risks that public agencies often cannot. I think there are some particularly good opportunities for smaller foundations in […]

mix_items.title: Could a short tail mean a new monkey species in Laos? Some scientists think so
mix_items.summary: There is no body. No genetic evidence — yet. There are just photos, but some scientists say those photos show a distinct enough primate to declare it a new species: the short-tailed langur, or Trachypithecus brevicaudus. The proposed species was described in the Vietnamese Journal of Primatology and lives in the Annamite Mountains of Laos. […]

mix_items.summary: Maribel Pacco grins as she recalls the first time she saw an Andean bear close-up in the wild. At the forest edge, a mother and her cubs browsed on bromeliads while the volunteer ranger watched for hours in awe. “I’m not a biologist, but at that moment, I decided to become a conservationist,” she says. mix_items.summary: ANTALYA, Turkey (AP) — Negotiators are still seeking concrete commitments for nations to transition away from fossil fuels, as this year’s U.N. climate summit reaches its final day. Friday marks the official end of this year’s two-week summit, known as COP31, which so far has failed to advance the drastic emission cuts needed to avert […]

mix_items.title: Japan looks to offshore wind to boost energy security, but hurdles remain
mix_items.summary: Japan has “tremendous potential” for offshore wind power, according to the national government and experts. But achieving that potential means overcoming major hurdles. While commercial-scale projects began coming online in recent years, the country still needs to address challenges that include refining its public-private partnerships, a buildout of related industries (such as turbine production), and […]

mix_items.title: Last Javan rhino habitat caught between mining plans and relocation debate
mix_items.summary: JAKARTA — Indonesian lawmakers and environmental groups are urging the government to revoke a mining map covering part of the waters around Ujung Kulon National Park, home to the world’s last surviving Javan rhinos. The calls were in response to a proposal by Hashim Djojohadikusumo, a mining and energy tycoon and the brother of President […]

mix_items.title: Fossil fuels’ role in Africa’s energy transition contested as UN climate conference closes
mix_items.summary: As the 2026 edition of the annual U.N. Climate Change Conference reaches its conclusion in Antalya, Türkiye, on Nov. 20, African governments are arguing for increased financial and technical support to respond to climate change. Top priorities include more money for protection of forests and other landscapes, funding to help vulnerable communities and economies adapt […]

mix_items.title: Nickel linked to deforestation in Indonesia traded on London Metal Exchange, says report
mix_items.summary: Two companies approved for trading nickel on the London Metal Exchange (LME) could be linked to supply chains that have cleared primary rainforest in Indonesia, according to a report published by the NGO Environmental Investigation Agency (EIA). The NGO investigated two LME-approved Indonesian refiners – PT CNGR Ding Xing and PT Eternal Nickel Industry (ENI) […]

mix_items.title: A mysterious 4,000-year-old wall is rewriting North Africa’s history
mix_items.summary: A remarkable 4,000-year-old defensive structure discovered in Morocco is rewriting what scientists thought they knew about ancient North African civilizations. The massive fortifications reveal unexpectedly sophisticated prehistoric societies and suggest that the region played a much greater role in Mediterranean history than previously recognized.
